items.title: ChatGPT blocks requests to imitate specific writers' styles
items.excerpt: OpenAI has begun blocking prompts asking ChatGPT to write in the style of specific living authors. Style isn't explicitly protected by copyright, but the change reshapes what writers can ask an AI to do.
items.rationale: A live product change that immediately narrows what any writer or editor can prompt for — the most directly actionable item in the pool.

items.title: AI-generated stories rated higher than human-written ones in new study
items.excerpt: A Cambridge University Press study found readers rated AI-generated stories higher than human-written ones — especially when they believed a human wrote them. The finding cuts at how publishers assess quality and how readers perceive authorship.
items.rationale: New peer-reviewed evidence that reader judgement of quality is decoupled from authorship — it reframes the whole 'human-written is better' assumption editors work from.

items.title: Anthropic found destroying books easier than negotiating copyright
items.excerpt: Rare-books curator Kathryn James on why Anthropic found destructively scanning 'all the books in the world' easier than negotiating copyright — and what that does to the physical record.
items.rationale: A rare-books curator's account of the physical cost of training-data acquisition — a distinct angle from the settlement coverage, and it names what is permanently lost.

items.title: The published voice: whose voice are we really reading?
items.excerpt: If AI is helping researchers write, what happens to 'author voice' — long a core consideration for authors, editors and reviewers? Roohi Ghosh unpacks how AI-assisted drafting reshapes editorial judgement.
items.rationale: Moves the debate from detection to craft: what editors and reviewers should actually be judging once drafting is machine-assisted.

items.title: Tor Bramble backs H M Wolfe after AI-detection claims over Daggermouth
items.excerpt: Tor Bramble is standing behind author HM Wolfe after The Atlantic reported that her dystopian romance Daggermouth scored 60% on the AI-detection tool Pangram. The case is becoming a test of whether detection scores can be trusted inside publishing workflows.
items.rationale: The first case of a publisher publicly refusing to act on a detection score — the counter-precedent to the pulled deals, and a real test of how much weight detection tools should carry.
